newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Angola looks to peace to boost coffee output.
newsitem.headline: Angola looks to peace to boost coffee output.

text.p: Angola, toppled by civil war as a top African coffee producer some 20 years ago, is banking on peace to boost its production over the next five years, an official said on Thursday.
Matesso Vicky, director of Angola's coffee institute, said the country planned to boost output to 50,000 tonnes by the year 2000 from a mere 5,000 tonnes in 1995/96 (October/September).
He said production in the 1996/97 coffee year was projected at 8,000 tonnes. It compares with peak production of 200,000 tonnes some two decades ago when it was ranked top producer in Africa.
"We were the number one producer in Africa about 20 years ago, and the third or fourth largest producer in the world," Vicky told Reuters on the tropical resort island of Bali.

Angola's government and former rebel UNITA movement fought a bloody 19-year civil war since independence from Portugal in 1975. Both sides signed a peace accord in the Zambian capital Lusaka in 1994 to end the fighting.
The transformation to peace is being overseen by 7,000 United Nations troops.

Vicky was attending a three-day meeting of the 61-member International Coffee Organization (ICO) which links producers and consuming countries. It was followed by a gathering of coffee producers from the Asia-Pacific region on Thursday.

African countries account for between 55 and 60 percent of the world's production of robusta coffee, which is known for its bitter flavour and is mixed with the more expensive arabica variety in portions that are considered a trade secret.
Angola has since been overtaken by African countries such as Uganda and the Ivory Coast as the continent's top producers.
"Our production started falling because of the fighting," Vicky said. "People did not have accessibility to their land as they were occupied by UNITA rebels."
"Most of the larger coffee growing areas were abandoned because of rebel occupation," he said. "But people with small plots continued to grow coffee."

Vicky said the government had undertaken a project to rehabilitate some 100,000 hectares of the total 500,000 hectares to boost production, and was offering technical and financial assistance to farmers.
He said that following the signing of the Lusaka peace accord, accessibility to coffee areas previously occupied by rebels was improving. "We are now able to work in the coffee areas again."
Vicky said, "We hope to earn about $100 million by the year 2000," adding that coffee was the country's second highest foreign exchange earner two decades ago after oil.
Diamonds have long replaced coffee as Angola's second highest export earner, he said.
"Even among African countries, we are now a very small producer of coffee," he added.
